movements.name: Art Nouveau
movements.blurb: 1890s–1910s. Whiplash curves, vines and flowers; nature as line.

movements.name: Art Deco
movements.blurb: 1920s–30s. Sunbursts, stepped forms, gold geometry of the machine-age luxury class.

movements.name: Psychedelia
movements.blurb: 1960s. Melting type, vibrating complementary colour, concert-poster swirl.

movements.name: Gothic Revival
movements.blurb: c. 1740s–1900s. Pointed arches and tracery again, from Walpole's Strawberry Hill to Pugin and the Houses of Parliament; for many, a religious and moral answer to the factory age.

movements.name: Ukiyo-e
movements.blurb: 17th–19th-century Japan. Woodblock prints of the "floating world": actors, courtesans, travellers, Hokusai's waves, sold cheap to city people.

movements.name: Minimalism
movements.blurb: 1960s on. Less, then less again: one line, one mark, a lot of air.

movements.name: Swiss / International
movements.blurb: 1950s. The grid, flush-left type, objective and clear.

movements.name: Bauhaus
movements.blurb: 1919–1933. Circle, square, triangle; art and industry as one school.

movements.name: Brutalism
movements.blurb: Raw concrete, exposed structure, no apology. Honest about what holds it up.

movements.name: Constructivism
movements.blurb: 1917–1930s. Art for the revolution: red wedges, diagonals, the poster as a tool.

movements.name: Dada
movements.blurb: 1916 on. Anti-art against a world that made the war. Nonsense as a weapon.

movements.name: Punk
movements.blurb: 1976 on. Photocopier, scissors, glue stick. Do it yourself because nobody will do it for you.

movements.name: Zine / DIY
movements.blurb: 1930s science-fiction fanzines, then punk from the 1970s: a photocopier, a stapler and something to say. Publishing without permission.

movements.name: Situationism
movements.blurb: 1957–1972. The Situationist International (Guy Debord, The Society of the Spectacle, 1967): hijack the ads, drift through the city, refuse the life on sale. Its slogans were on the walls of Paris in May 1968.

movements.name: Grunge Design
movements.blurb: Late 1980s–1990s. Distressed type and broken layouts, from Seattle gig flyers to David Carson's Ray Gun (1992 on). Legibility on purpose made second.

movements.name: Futurism
movements.blurb: 1909. Speed, engines, noise. (Its founders also loved war; read the manifestos critically.)

movements.name: Cyberpunk
movements.blurb: 1980s on. High tech, low life. Neon over rain, corporations over everything.

movements.name: Vaporwave
movements.blurb: 2010s. Mall music, dead tech, a sunset that never ends. Nostalgia for a future sold to us.

movements.name: Afrofuturism
movements.blurb: Sun Ra's Arkestra from the 1950s, Octavia Butler, Parliament-Funkadelic; named by Mark Dery in 1993. Black futures imagined by the people the official future left out. A way of seeing more than a single style.

movements.name: Y2K
movements.blurb: Late 1990s–early 2000s. Translucent plastic, chrome blobs and bubble buttons: the glossy millennium the dot-com boom was selling. The name came later.

movements.name: Maximalism
movements.blurb: More is more. Pattern on pattern, colour on colour, nothing left empty.

movements.name: Pop Art
movements.blurb: 1950s–60s. Soup cans and comic panels; the market's own images turned back on it.

movements.name: Memphis
movements.blurb: 1981–1987. Ettore Sottsass's Milan group: plastic laminate, squiggles, clashing pattern, furniture that laughed at good taste.

movements.name: Abstract Expressionism
movements.blurb: 1940s–50s. The gesture is the subject: drips, slashes, the body on the canvas.

movements.name: Geometric Abstraction
movements.blurb: Pure shape and colour relationships, from Malevich to Albers.

movements.name: Op Art
movements.blurb: 1960s. Patterns that make the eye do the moving.

movements.name: Surrealism
movements.blurb: 1924 on. André Breton's manifesto: dreams, automatic writing, the uncanny next to the ordinary. In 1938 Breton and Trotsky wrote the Manifesto for an Independent Revolutionary Art together (Breton and Diego Rivera signed it).

movements.name: Expressionism
movements.blurb: c. 1905–1920s. Die Brücke (1905) and Der Blaue Reiter (1911) bent form and colour to show what a thing feels like, not what it looks like. The Nazis branded it "degenerate art" in 1937.
